---
title: "Lab 3 — Spot the error"
subtitle: "Day Three · 25 min"
---

Checking your own draft is easy to skip, because you already believe it. Checking someone else's output cold is closer to the real job: most of what reaches you in a working week, from a tool or a colleague, is text you did not write. This lab is practice at doing that with a card and a source, and nothing else. The loop is short: underline the claims, find three of them in a source you open, mark each one.

::: {.session-meta}
Time
:   25 minutes, two parts: trade and catch 15; instructor examples 10

Slides
:   [Open the deck](../slides/lab3-spot-the-error.qmd): the same lab, one step to a slide, with the pictures.

Uses
:   The output you saved in [Lab 1, part 2](../day1/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd#part-2); the verification card in [Module 6](m6-confidently-wrong.qmd#confidently-wrong)

You leave with
:   Practice at finding an error you were not told about, and a five-minute peer-check you can run at work.
:::

## 1. Trade and catch [15 min]{.time} {#part-1}

You will swap the answer you saved in Lab 1 with a partner in a breakout room and try to find what is wrong with theirs. You use only the verification card from Module 6. No breakout room on your call? Then check your own saved output instead, cold, as if someone else had written it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Their output"] --> B["Underline<br/>every claim"]
    B --> C["Pick the three<br/>that matter most"]
    C --> D["Find each one<br/>in a source you open"]
    D --> E["Mark it:<br/>confirmed, wrong,<br/>could-not-find"]
    classDef step fill:#EEF2FF,stroke:#4F46E5,color:#0F172A
    classDef pick fill:#EEF2FF,stroke:#4F46E5,stroke-width:3px,color:#0F172A
    classDef out fill:#CCFBF1,stroke:#14B8A6,color:#0F172A
    class A,B step
    class C pick
    class D,E out
```

### Get your output ready

Open the output you saved in Lab 1, part 2. Its first line should read:

```text
PRACTICE OUTPUT: CONTAINS DELIBERATELY UNRELIABLE CONTENT. NOT FOR CLINICAL USE.
```

**Did not save one?** Run a fresh probe now (the five papers prompt from [Lab 1, part 2](../day1/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd#part-2)), copy the answer into a note, and type that warning line at the top yourself. It takes a couple of minutes; do it while the others do the same.

Nothing you swap should contain patient information. A probe is a question, not a patient. If yours has anything about a real person in it, do not swap it.

### The protocol

1. **Swap (1 min).** In your breakout room, paste the output and the question you asked to get it into the breakout chat for your partner. Do not say what you found when you checked it in Lab 1.
2. **Check cold (9 min).** Underline the claims (3 minutes), then find three of them in a source you open and mark each (6 minutes). Record as you go in the table below.
3. **Compare (3 min).** Send it back. Where your findings differ from theirs, each say how you checked. The disagreements are the useful part.
4. **Reflect (2 min).** Answer the question at the end of this part, in your notes.

**The rules for checking.** Do not ask an AI tool whether the output is right, and do not ask its owner. Use a search engine, your library, your formulary, or your institution's guideline to find primary sources. A literature-grounded tool can point you to a paper, but a claim is confirmed only when you have read it there yourself. Could-not-find counts as wrong, and so does any claim you did not reach.

### Underline, then pick three

Underline every number, name, date, dose and citation in the output. This is step 1 of the card, and the step people skip because it is tedious. You will not get to every claim in the time. Pick the **three** that would matter most if they were wrong, and start there.

### Where to look first

| If the claim is | Look first in |
|---|---|
| A guideline recommendation, threshold, or number | The guideline document itself, as its issuing body published it, not a summary |
| A dosing or interaction statement | The drug's product label, or your institution's formulary |
| A statistic or a study finding | The paper: the abstract for the claim, the results for the number |
| A citation | Whether the paper exists, and whether it says what the output says it does |
| A local policy or protocol | Your institution's own document |

### Record what you find

Copy this into your notes. Three rows are enough.

| # | Claim, in the output's own words | Where I looked | Mark |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| 3 | | | |

For each mark, write confirmed, wrong, or could-not-find. For each one that is wrong, add the kind of error: **invented**, **omitted**, **altered**, or a **fabricated citation**.

If you find nothing wrong, say how you know: list what you confirmed and where you found it. A clean result you cannot show is not yet a clean result. If the output is a refusal or mostly hedging, note what the tool said it could not do, then use one that is not.

### What would have caught it faster?

Write two or three lines. Two questions to start from:

- Which claim could I have checked in under a minute, and why did I not start there?
- What would I change in my own prompt? For example, add to CONSTRAINTS: *Do not cite sources or guidelines; I will supply them.*

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Watch for
The pull to paste the output into a tool and ask "what is wrong with this?" You get a second draft, not a check. The card works because you are the one who finds the source.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
Underline the claims first, then check them one at a time: an error you have not looked for stays invisible.
:::

## 2. Instructor examples [10 min]{.time} {#part-2}

Your instructor will share one or two short examples prepared in advance, so the whole group checks the same text. They are on the shared screen only. The examples and their answers are not on this page, because seeing them first would spoil the practice. The topics are fictional and carry no patient information.

### Procedure

1. **Read it twice (2 min).** First, underline every checkable claim and copy them onto your table: step 1 of the card. Then read the text against itself: do its parts agree with each other?
2. **Check (3 min).** On your own, work down the card. Where there is no source to open, say which source you would go to and mark the claim could-not-find.
3. **Call it (3 min).** The instructor asks for findings. For each, give three things: the claim, how you would confirm it, and the kind of error.
4. **Score yourself (2 min).** After the instructor's key, count what you found and what you missed, and write down which kind of error you missed.

With two examples, each gets half the time.

### Reflect

Which kind of error did you find fastest, and which did you walk past? If you missed an omission, remember that it cannot be seen by checking what is on the page. Read the source against the output, as in step 3 of the card.

### Run a peer-check at work

The same routine works between two colleagues, in about five minutes:

1. The author hands over the AI output and the source it was drafted from, and nothing else: no opinion about whether it is good.
2. The checker works down the verification card, cold.
3. The checker reports each finding as claim, mark, and kind of error, not "looks fine".
4. The author makes the changes and decides what is used. AI drafts. You decide.

Use it where the stakes are highest: doses, allergies, diagnoses, and anything going into a chart. Send the text through your institution's own channels. If it contains anything about a patient, never send it through a personal messaging app or a consumer AI tool ([Module 7](m7-privacy.qmd#the-rule)).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
For anything that matters, get a second person to check it cold before you use it.
:::
